Below is a structured, detailed description of the “Input Description” table from the BDK Buckling Resistance manual.  Use this summary to guide ingestion into a RAG-based vector store or to understand exactly what kinds of input records and parameters the BDK solver expects.

1.  Input Description Overview  
    – Chapter in manual: “3 Input Description” (pp. 3-1 ff.)  
    – Purpose: defines every record/statement through which the user feeds geometry, support conditions, materials, design-code parameters, loadcases, selected members and output controls into the BDK buckling-resistance task.

2.  Sections and Record Types  
    3.1  Input Language  
        •  Specifies the syntax conventions (keywords, field separators, continuation rules).  
    3.2  Input Records  
        •  Lists all record names (CVA, CVE, CVM, CVL, CV, TVAR, CTRL, LC, MEMB, ECHO) with a one-line summary.  
    3.3  Conversion of Projects  
        3.3.1 CADINP Commands  
            •  Legacy-conversion commands to adapt older STAR2/AQUA input into BDK.

3.  Support-Definition Records  
    3.4  CVA – Support at the Beginning  
        •  Defines translational (u,v,w) and rotational (about local axes) restraints at the “start” node of each individual beam element.  
        •  Optional elastic‐warping stiffness.  
    3.5  CVE – Support at the End  
        •  Same fields as CVA but applied to the “end” node of the beam.  
    3.6  CVM – Intermediate Support  
        •  Inserts a set of point supports along the beam span (fractional or absolute coordinate).  
    3.7  CVL – Lateral Restraints  
        •  Applies lateral (out‐of‐plane) springs or braces at defined positions.  
        •  Includes torsional spring stiffness if warping restraint is needed.  
    3.8  CV – Continuous Support  
        •  Applies uniform spring support distributed along the entire beam length.  
        •  Fields: translational springs, rotational springs, warping‐torsion springs.

4.  Parameterization Records  
    3.9  TVAR – Template Variables  
        •  Declare user‐defined named scalars (real or integer).  
        •  Allow reuse in subsequent records (e.g. TVAR L=6.0, B=0.3 → MEMB definitions).

5.  Controlling Parameters  
    3.10  CTRL – Controlling Parameters  
        •  Global flags and default values that influence how BDK interprets the model and executes checks.  
        •  Typical fields:  
            – NORM: select design code (EN 1993-1-1, DIN 18800-2/OEN 4300, BS 5950).  
            – BUCK_TYPE: LTB vs. pure lateral.  
            – WARPING: on/off, stiffness factors.  
            – TAPERED: allowance for section taper.  
            – EFFECTIVE: compute effective section (class 4 per EN 1993).  
        3.10.1 EN 1993–1-1 sub-section (ctrl fields specific to Eurocode 3)  
        3.10.2 DIN 18800–2 / OEN 4300 sub-section  
        3.10.3 BS 5950 sub-section  

6.  Selection Records  
    3.11  LC – Loadcase Selection  
        •  Identifies which loadcases (from STAR2/AQUA analysis) are to be used for the buckling‐eigenvalue problem.  
        •  Fields: LCID, scale factor, description.  
    3.12  MEMB – Member Selection  
        •  Lists element IDs (beams or trusses) extracted from the global model.  
        •  Can specify ranges, wildcards, or explicit lists.  

7.  Output Control  
    3.13  ECHO – Control of Output  
        •  Toggles printing of input echo, detailed intermediate results, summary tables.  
        •  Fields: ECHO=ALL/BRIEF/NONE, destination (listing, external file), format options.

Summary of Usage Flow:  
– Define any TVARs you need.  
– Set CTRL to choose your code, buckling-type, warping and effective-section options.  
– Specify support conditions with CVA/CVE (end supports), CVM (mid-span), CVL (lateral items) or CV (distributed).  
– Point BDK to your analysis loadcase via LC.  
– Specify which members to check via MEMB.  
– Control verbosity and output format via ECHO.  

This table of input records ensures that BDK can build and solve the eigenvalue problem for any straight‐member stability check, accommodate general cross‐sections (including class-4 thin‐walled), and apply the correct design-code formulas for ultimate‐load buckling resistance.

 1 Task Description
 BDK provides solution to the problem of beam stability. It determines the stability eigenvalues for buckling of a straight individual member. The member, which is taken from the entire sys- tem, is calculated with STAR2 or ASE and the buckling resistance check of steel members is performed according to the specified design code.
 1.1 Task Outline
 At first, the user defines the system selecting straight, individual beam or truss elements, which are cut out of the entire structural system and are treated independently. The program allows the user to explicitly define the support conditions at the start and end of each selected indi- vidual beam, as well as continuous supports, offering a complete control on the properties of the selected system. Furthermore, standards-related design parameters may also be explicitly defined.
 Having available the complete system, the program sets up and solves the formed stability eigenvalue problem and the eigenvalues and eigenforms are determined for a pre-specified and calculated loadcase. Following the eigenvalues determination and taking into considera- tion the defined design parameters, BDK performs the buckling check according to the selected design code.
 1.2 Supported Design Codes
 The design checks are performed according to one of the following supported standards:
 • DIN 18800-2 / OEN 4300: Structural steelwork analysis of safety against buckling of linear members and frames [1].
 • EN 1993-1-1: Design of steel structures - Part 1-1: General rules and rules for buildings [2].
 • BS 5950-1: Structural use of steelwork in building [3].
 1.3 Assumptions and Limitations
 BDK can determine the stability eigenvalues under the following assumptions:
 • General, also unsymmetric cross-sections
 • General tapered sections (along the beam axis)
 • Straight beam axis and centric haunches
 • Change of the boundary conditions including the elastic warping constraint and distributed support.

1.3 Assumptions and Limitations. BDK can determine the stability eigenvalues under the following assumptions:. • General, also unsymmetric cross-sections. • General tapered sections (along the beam axis). • Straight beam axis and centric haunches. • Change of the boundary conditions including the elastic warping constraint and distributed support..
 • Solution for the complete lateral torsional buckling problem or for the plain lateral buckling problem with disregard of the normal force.
 For the calculation of the lateral torsional buckling safety for an individual beam, according to DIN 18800-2, the assumptions of this design code hold. This implies that the design is strictly valid only for double symmetric I and H sections, without the intended torsional loading.
 Materials, section profiles and the design code to comply with, are selected by the user at the early steps of defining the total structural system. Regardless of the initial design standard selection, the user may explicitly redefine in the BDK task the specification of a different design standard (see NORM). This practice should be done with caution, since significant differences exist between the design codes, regarding material mechanical behaviour and properties as well as the considered safety factors.
 Furthermore, a cross-section of class 4 of EN 1993-1-1 and EN 1993-1-5 can be treated, since the calculation of the effective cross-section values in BDK is available.
 Warning
 At the current version of BDK, it is possible to calculate only the effective properties for THIN-WALLED cross-sections (Iterative Method). Another approach would be to use the SIG NEFF input in AQUA, which works both for solid, as well as for thin-walled cross- sections. Please refer to the VERIFICATION Manual Design - Example DCE-EN 30.
 For the determination of the critical force and moment for buckling, always an eigenvalue anal- ysis is performed, except of explicitly user-defined buckling lengths. In the unlikely event that the eigenvalue analysis fails, analytical formulas are used.

A model system can consist of several beam or truss elements, forming a member, although there are no individual supports between its endings, other than the optionally defined. The user can select any straight beam or truss element to cut out of the entire structural system. Each selected member is then treated by BDK as an individual independent system, taking into account the inner forces and displacements derived from the parental system analysis for a considered loadcase. For a member that represents a subsystem of the total system, the corresponding support conditions have to be defined carefully. This applies in particular to the sway perpendicular to the system plane, for the case where the system was entered as a planar system.

The start and end boundary conditions can be defined using the CVA and CVE input. With- out this specification, they are set to Fork-Fork. Moreover, BDK assumes that there are no intermediate individual supports between the endings of the selected member, other than the optionally defined intermediate supports (CVM), lateral restraints (CVL), and continuous sup- ports (CV). Therefore, the user should explicitly enter the exact boundary conditions at both ends (CVA / CVE) and in between them (CVM / CVL / CV). For this purpose, different input options are available:
 the assignment of spring constant values,
 the definition of fixities using the literal FIX,
 •
 the automatic computation of the spring constant values using the literal AUTO.
 •
 The supports thus defined are oriented in the local directions of the member.
 In the case of the literal AUTO, the corresponding spring constant value of a support is auto- matically determined by a linear analysis of the global structure. This value is independent of the design load case. Hence, imperfections or second order effects are not incorporated. It should be also noted that the supports only constrain single degrees of freedom and do not couple them. Therefore, coupling effects are considered in a simplified way. Between different nodes, coupling effects are neglected. The literal AUTO can be used in the CVA, CVE, and CVM input.
 The automatic calculation of the boundary conditions (AUTO) supports parallel processing of the elements and uses a parallel finite element solver. This means, that the performance may be improved by using multicore processors.
 Hint
 See Example 58 of the VERIFICATION Manual Mechanical for a demonstration of the automatic computation of the spring constant values.

 A member rotated about the longitudinal axis can be modelled by rotating the cross sec- tion with the ALPH input in AQUA instead of rotating the local coordinate system of the member using the DROT input in SOFIMSHA/C. In this way, the supports defined in BDK, which refer to the local coordinate system of the member, can be better aligned to the boundary conditions of the global structure, such as fixities.

Literature and design codes distinguish between the following cases for beam structures:
 • Lateral Torsional Buckling: the most general case of buckling where deflections towards both axes as well as torsional rotation (twist) occur.
 • Lateral Buckling: lateral deflection and torsional rotation (twist).
 • Flexural Buckling: buckling about the strong or weak axis, in-plane deformation, no tor- sional rotation.
 • Torsional Buckling: buckling about the longitudinal axis, torsional rotation (twist), the beam axis remain straight.

The figure is a two-dimensional Cartesian plot of the buckling reduction factor χ (vertical axis) as a function of the non-dimensional slenderness λ̄ (horizontal axis), presenting the five characteristic “buckling curves” a₀, a, b, c and d as specified in EN 1993-1-1 (Eurocode 3 for steel structures).  

Axes and Grid  
 • The horizontal axis is labeled “λ̄” and spans from 0.0 at the left up to 2.3 at the right, with major tick marks (and light grey grid lines) at 0.2-unit intervals.  
 • The vertical axis is labeled “χ” and runs from 0.0 at the bottom up to 1.1 at the top, with major ticks (and grid lines) every 0.1 unit.  
 • A light-grey background grid covers the plotting area, reinforcing both axes’ tick intervals and aiding the eye in reading off pairs of (λ̄, χ).  

Buckling Curves  
 • All five curves originate at the point (λ̄ = 0, χ = 1.0), reflecting that perfectly stubby elements (zero slenderness) carry full elastic capacity.  
 • As λ̄ increases, each curve slopes downward in an “S-like” fashion: gently at first, then more steeply for λ̄ roughly between 0.6 and 1.4, before flattening out toward the right.  
 • The topmost curve, labeled a₀, gives the highest χ values at any given λ̄, indicating the least sensitivity to slenderness. Immediately below it is curve a, then b, then c, and finally the lowest curve d. This ordering reflects increasingly conservative (lower) reduction factors for more imperfection-sensitive cross-section classes or imperfection amplitudes.  
 • By λ̄ ≈ 2.0–2.2, all five curves have converged close to χ ≈ 0.15–0.20, indicating that for very slender sections the allowable buckling capacity becomes small and nearly independent of the precise imperfection category.  

Styling and Annotation  
 • Each curve is drawn as a smooth, solid black line of uniform thickness. Adjacent curves are labeled by their letter designations (“a₀,” “a,” “b,” “c,” “d”) placed roughly mid-span on each line, slanted to follow the curve’s slope.  
 • The axes’ labels and the legend annotations use a serif font consistent with technical typesetting.  
 • Beneath the plot, centered, is the caption “Figure 2.1: Buckling curves according to EN 1993-1-1.”  

Contextual Role  
In the broader design methodology (referenced in Petersen [4], Roik–Carl–Lindner [5], and extended by Schroeter [6]), these χ vs. λ̄ curves encapsulate geometric-nonlinear (imperfection-sensitive) buckling effects. They provide the reduction factor applied to the elastic critical load in order to obtain a realistic ultimate buckling resistance for slender steel members under compression. This approach bridges the gap between purely elastic-stability theory (which ignores material yielding) and plastic design rules (which ignore geometric nonlinearities), forming a key part of the energy-based variational formulation implemented in advanced structural-stability software.

The case of buckling will occur if an element will suffer from large forces due to small defor- mations induced by geometric non-linear effects. This will limit the ultimate load for slender structures.
 The elasto-static theory of stability will not account for material non-linearities, while the stan- dard plastic design method will not account for the geometric non-linearities. As both theories are not applicable in a general case, their results will define basic design parameters used for the combined design of the effects.
 For the quite general case treated within the program a solution based on an analytical ap- proach is no longer available. The solution is obtained by a variational approach based on the energy. The expression of the energy comprehends quite a lot of terms and is given and explained in detail in the book of Petersen [4] (eq. 7.65 page 675) or Roik, Carl, and Lindner [5]. BDK uses an extended formulation according to Schroeter [6].

The image is a 2-D schematic of a hot-rolled equal-leg angle section, presented in plan view and annotated to show both its principal axes (y-y and z-z) and its geometric axes (u-u and v-v). It is labeled “Figure 2.2: Axes of angle section.”

General geometry and coloring  
• The section outline is drawn with a continuous red line. It forms an L-shape with one vertical leg rising from the lower left corner and one horizontal leg extending to the right from that same corner.  
• The inner corner of the L-section is sharply defined (no fillet radius), but five small red ticks mark subdivision points along each leg.  
• At two locations—one on the vertical leg and one on the horizontal leg—magenta asterisks denote reference points, perhaps mid-points or check points for section properties.  
• Along the bottom of the vertical leg, slightly above the inner corner, a small yellow circle containing the letters “SC” is placed (suggesting the shear center or another special point).

Axes and centroid  
• The centroid of the cross-section is indicated by a yellow ring centered on a tiny crosshair symbol. From that point, four dashed brown lines radiate outward: two align with the global Cartesian axes (horizontal and vertical) and two lie along intermediate, rotated directions.  
• The horizontal dashed line is labeled “y” near its rightward end; the vertical dashed line is labeled “z” immediately above its upward extension. Together they define the principal axes y-y (horizontal) and z-z (vertical) of the section.  
• Two additional dashed lines are drawn crossing at the same centroid: one slopes upward to the right and is labeled “u,” the other slopes downward to the right and is labeled “v.” These denote the geometric axes u-u and v-v, which for angle sections generally represent the axes of symmetry or maximum/minimum second moments of area.

Annotations and context  
• The red ticks along the legs likely mark equal subdivisions or control points used in numerical shape representation.  
• The yellow “SC” circle on the vertical leg hints at the shear-center location, relevant when locating loads that induce only bending without twisting.  
• Magenta asterisks may indicate special measurement points for cross-section properties or buckling checks.  
• The caption at the bottom reads “Figure 2.2: Axes of angle section,” tying the graphic back to the text’s discussion of principal-axis orientation in Eurocode beam-stability checks.  

Interpretation relative to Eurocode context  
• The image visually emphasizes that for nonsymmetric sections like angles, the principal neutral axes (y-y and z-z) do not coincide with the geometric symmetry axes (u-u and v-v).  
• In the context of EN 1993-1-1, Section 6.3.3 (combined bending and axial compression), interaction checks must refer to principal properties about y-y and z-z. Even though the section’s “natural” axes might be u-u and v-v, the code requires evaluation about the true principal axes, as illustrated here.  
• This figure thus underpins the BDK software’s approach: always perform buckling and bending–compression interaction checks about the principal axes y-y and z-z, irrespective of any other axis system used to define the shape.

Eurocode’s approach to the beam stability design checks depends mostly on two important factors:
 1. The type of loading:
 (a) Compressive axial force (EN 1993-1-1, 6.3.1)
 (b) Major axis bending moment (EN 1993-1-1, 6.3.2)
 (c) Combined bending and axial compression (EN 1993-1-1, 6.3.3)
 The type, shape and properties of the cross-section.
 BDK performes the design check for the combined bending and axial compression, as it is described in EN 1993-1-1, 6.3.3, Eq. 6.61 and 6.62 with the interaction factors kyy, kyz, kzy, kzz. Interaction factors are calculated according to Method 1 (1993-1-1, Annex A) or Method 2 (EN 1993-1-1, Annex B).
 all rules relate to principal axis properties, which are generally defined by the axes ”y-y” and ”z-z”, but for the sections such as angles are defined by the axes ”u-u” and ”v-v”, as shown in Fig. 2.2. BDK performs the check with respect to ”y-y” and ”z-z” and not ”u-u” and ”v-v”.
 A more pictorial representation of the design algorithm according to EN 1993-1-1, for compres- sion and for bending can be visualised in Fig. 2.3 and 2.4.
 As mentioned earlier, for the determination of the critical load Ncr and moment Mcr, an eigen- value analysis is performed. In the unlikely event that the eigenvalue analysis fails, e.g. due to non adequate input of the system definition, a fallback solution with approximatively analytical formulas is used. The image is a schematic flowchart (titled “Figure 2.3: Flexural Buckling”) illustrating the step-by-step procedure prescribed in EN 1993-1-1 for determining the buckling resistance of a doubly-symmetric member under axial compression with possible bending (i.e. flexural buckling). Below is a detailed walk-through of its elements and logical connections:

1. Top block (process box)  
   • “Eigenvalue Analysis – only axial force (Ncr)”  
   – This is the starting point: an eigenvalue (finite-element or analytical) calculation of the pure-axial critical force.  

2. First decision (diamond)  
   • “Input of SKy and SKz?”  
   – SKy, SKz represent lateral restraint stiffnesses about the y- and z-axes.  
   – If “Yes,” the flow loops back to a later stage (the Euler-formula path), indicating that these spring stiff­nesses can be included later.  
   – If “No,” proceed downward to check whether the eigen­value analysis succeeded.  

3. Second decision (diamond)  
   • “Eig. Anal. successful?”  
   – If “Yes,” go to the next box  
   – If “No,” branch to the “Euler Formula” block  

4. Euler-formula path (process box)  
   • “Euler Formula”  
   – Used whenever the eigenvalue analysis fails or is not invoked; calculates the classical Euler buckling load Ncr based on pinned-end length, moment of inertia, material E, etc.  

5. Trapezoid (data/output)  
   • “Critical force Ncr”  
   – Whether obtained via eigenvalue analysis or via the Euler formula, the resulting critical force Ncr is the starting point for slenderness evaluation.  

6. Non-dimensional slenderness (process box)  
   • “Calculate non-dimensional slenderness λ, EN 1993-1-1, 6.3.2”  
   – λ = √(A·f0,y / Ncr) or another equivalent form, depending on section class and reference stress f0,y.  

7. Buckling curve selection (process box)  
   • “Determine buckling curve EN 1993-1-1, Table 6.5 (or Table 6.4 for general case or section classes G1–G3)”  
   – Select the appropriate buckling imperfection curve (a, b, c, etc.) according to cross-section type and end-restraint conditions.  

8. Imperfection factor (process box)  
   • “Imperfection factor α, EN 1993-1-1, Table 6.1”  
   – α quantifies initial out-of-straightness or residual stress imperfection magnitude for the chosen curve.  

9. Calculation of Φ (process box)  
   • “Calculate Φ, EN 1993-1-1, Table 6.x”  
   – Φ is an intermediate factor defined by Φ = [1 + α·(λ – 0.2) + λ²] / 8 (or analogous formula) per the standard’s tables.  

10. Reduction factor χ (process box)  
    • “Calculate reduction factor χ ≤ 1.0, EN 1993-1-1, Eq. 6.57 (or 6.56, 6.58 for modified forms)”  
    – χ = 1 / [Φ + √(Φ² – λ²)], limited to a maximum of 1.0.  Modified factors (χmod) account for end moments or lateral restraints, if applicable.  

11. Design buckling resistance (process box)  
    • “Calculate design buckling resistance Nb,Rd, EN 1993-1-1, 6.3.2.1(3)”  
    – Nb,Rd = χ·A·fy / γM1, where fy is the design yield strength and γM1 the partial safety factor.  

12. End box  
    • “Design buckling resistance Nb,Rd”  
    – Final output: the governing buckling resistance for ultimate limit state design.  

Loop-backs and Optional Steps:  
– If SKy and SKz are defined, the chart indicates the Euler-formula path may re-enter the slenderness evaluation stage with modified boundary conditions (i.e. accounting for lateral support springs).  
– In a fully coupled eigenvalue solution with lateral‐torsional restraints (Annex B Method 2 of EN 1993-1-1), one would supply these spring stiffnesses directly and produce Ncr considering both flexural and torsional buckling modes.

– Rectangles/process boxes = computational steps (e.g. calculate λ)

The analysis procedure for the lateral torsional buckling design is made according to DIN 18800, Part 2 Element 301, where it says: For the simplification of beams, continuous beams and frames, one can evaluate flexural buckling and lateral torsional buckling separately. Whereby the flexural buckling analysis is followed by the lateral torsional buckling analysis. Each analysis is made for individual beams, which are picked from the entire system. Each beam is subjected to the beam-end internal forces and moments, which are determined for the entire system.
 The flexural buckling analysis is made with the programs STAR2 or ASE. All the individual beams, of the system being analysed for flexural buckling, are provided with support conditions, usually torsional restraints are applied. The STAR2 or ASE calculation has to be made with ultimate loads or γ-factor loads. Whereby the analysis procedure elastic-elastic or plastic- plastic (non-linear theory) according to DIN 18800, Part 2 Table 101 is possible in STAR2 or ASE. All the elasto-plastic regions must be fixed laterally against torsion and deformation, which is required for the conservation of the cross-section.
 The individual checks are then calculated with the equations from the elements 310, 318 and 321 of the DIN 18800-2.

The table under review defines six elemental support‐spring parameters that BDK employs when establishing fork‐support conditions on beam elements. These parameters are only “activated” when you follow them immediately with a MEMB input, and they govern how the beam’s local translational and rotational degrees of freedom interact with elastic springs or rigid fixities. In the context of BDK, positive parameter values specify spring stiffness, negative values (–1.0 or the literal FIX) impose a rigid support, and the literal AUTO instructs BDK to compute an appropriate spring constant automatically. See also the CVE and CVA cards for related connectivity and cross‐section assignments.

1. Item Codes and Physical Meaning  
   • CB – Spring constant for warping bi‐moment. This parameter resists “warping” deformations along the beam’s longitudinal axis by providing a torsional‐warping stiffness.  
   • CY – Spring constant for lateral displacement in the local Y‐direction. It represents a translational spring that resists transverse shear in Y.  
   • CZ – Spring constant for lateral displacement in the local Z‐direction. Analogous to CY, but acting in the beam’s Z lateral axis.  
   • DX – Rotational spring constant for pure torsion about the beam’s longitudinal (X) axis. It couples the twist angle to an internal torsional moment.  
   • DY – Rotational spring constant for bending about the local Y‐axis (Moment My). This provides a rotational restraint to bending in the Y‐plane.  
   • DZ – Rotational spring constant for bending about the local Z‐axis (Moment Mz). It serves the same role as DY, but for bending in the Z‐plane.

2. Units  
   • CB is given in kN·m³, corresponding to a warping‐moment per unit warping rotation.  
   • CY and CZ each use kN/m, consistent with a force per unit lateral displacement.  
   • DX, DY, and DZ are all in kN·m/rad, specifying the moment resisted per unit rotation about the respective axis.

3. Default Values and Behavioral Implications  
   • CB defaults to 0. A zero stiffness here means no warping restraint unless explicitly defined.  
   • CY and CZ default to ∞ (infinite stiffness), effectively clamping lateral translations in Y and Z by default. Users must override this if they want an elastic lateral support.  
   • DX defaults to ∞, implying a rigid torsional support unless changed or set to AUTO.  
   • DY and DZ both default to 0, indicating no rotational spring resistance about the Y or Z axes unless specified.

4. Special Literals  
   • FIX or –1.0: Forces a fully rigid constraint in that degree of freedom, overriding any numerical value.  
   • AUTO: Delegates the choice of an appropriate stiffness value to BDK’s internal algorithm, useful for scenarios where a semi‐rigid support model is desired without manually estimating spring constants.

5. Application Notes  
   – These inputs must immediately precede a MEMB entry to take effect.  
   – The combination of translational springs (CY, CZ) and rotational springs (DX, DY, DZ), plus warping bi‐moment (CB), allows detailed modelling of semi‐rigid supports such as soil springs, bearings, or flexible connections.  
   – Always cross‐check with CVE (element connectivity) and CVA/CVA cards (alignment and orientation) to ensure that “local directions” align with the intended global geometry.  

This table thus provides a concise but flexible mechanism for engineers to define a range of support conditions—from fully fixed to selectively elastic—in a single, unified input block.

See also: CVE, MEMB
 CVA
 As a default BDK employs a fork support condition.
 The supports are in the local directions of the beam and are defined as spring constants (positive values) or as fixities (negative values). The value -1.0 or the literal FIX represent a fixed constraint. The literal AUTO enables the automatic computation of a spring constant value.
 These input values are active only for the subsequent MEMB input.

The table shown defines the spring‐support parameters that may be applied, in the local coordinate system of a beam element, when you issue a MEMB entry in BDK.  These parameters control how the beam “sees” supports in six degrees of freedom—three translations (along local y and z axes plus warping in x) and three rotations (about local x, y and z).  By default, BDK employs what it calls a “fork support” condition; the entries in this table override or augment that default for the subsequent MEMB record only.  Positive values are interpreted as linear (or rotational) spring constants; negative values (–1.0 or the literal FIX) impose a fully fixed constraint; and the literal AUTO tells BDK to compute an appropriate stiffness automatically.

Column definitions  
• Item  
  – The two‐letter code that you use on your MEMB card to specify that particular support stiffness.  
• Description  
  – A brief explanation of which degree of freedom the spring term affects.  
• Unit

The table defines the syntax and meaning of the CVL (“constraint‐at‐a‐local‐station”) input card, which allows you to impose spring‐type supports or full fixities at arbitrary points along a beam member.  These CVL definitions remain in effect for all subsequent MEMB cards until changed.  You do not need a finite‐element mesh node exactly at the specified station; CVL will internally locate or create the necessary constraint point.  

Below is a breakdown of each column and row in the table, together with the overall context in which CVL is used:

1. Overall Context  
   • CVL is used in the +PROG BDK input deck, typically placed before one or more MEMB definitions.  
   • Each CVL line defines one support or spring constraint in the beam’s local coordinate system.  
   • Positive values for CY and DX are spring constants (stiffness).  
   • A value of –1.0 or the literal FIX indicates a fully fixed constraint in that degree of freedom.  

2. Columns  
   • Item: the keyword or parameter name you must supply.  
   • Description: what the parameter means and any special options.  
   • Unit: the physical units or data type of the parameter.  
   • Default: value assumed if you omit the parameter or use ‘*’.  

3. Row‐by‐Row Detail  

   a) REF  (Unit: LIT; Default: *)  
      – “Reference” location on the member where this CVL entry applies.  You must choose one of four literal codes:  
         • STRT — measured from the start (first end) of the member  
         • MID  — measured from the midpoint of the member  
         • END  — measured from the end (second end) of the member  
         • XI   — a relative coordinate between start (0) and end (1)  
      – This field is required.  If omitted or ‘*’, CVL is not applied.  

   b) S  (Unit: m or – for XI; Default: 0)  
      – Offset distance along the member local axis from the chosen REF point.  
      – For REF=STRT, MID or END, S is in meters.  For REF=XI, S is a dimensionless fraction [0, 1].  
      – Default of 0 means exactly at the reference location.  

   c) CY  (Unit: kN/m; Default: 0)  
      – Linear spring constant resisting lateral displacement in the local y-direction.  
      – CY > 0 imposes a lateral spring.  CY = 0 means no lateral spring.  
      – CY = –1.0 or FIX means fully restrain the local‐y translation (i.e. pinned in that direction).  

   d) DX  (Unit: kNm/rad; Default: 0)  
      – Rotational spring constant around the local-x axis (torsion).  
      – DX > 0 imposes a torsional (about-x) spring.  DX = 0 means free rotation.  
      – DX = –1.0 or FIX means fully fix the torsional rotation.  

   e) HDIV  (Unit: –; Default: *)  
      – “Homogeneous DIVision” parameter.  If specified as an integer N > 1, the member is subdivided into N equal finite‐element segments at this point.  
      – Use this when you want to guarantee an FEM node exactly at the CVL location.  
      – If omitted or ‘*’, no additional partitioning occurs beyond what is automatically required.  

4. Usage Example  
   +PROG BDK  
     …  
     CVL REF STRT S 1.0 CY FIX DX FIX   ! a fully fixed support 1 m from the start  
     CVL REF MID  S 0.5 CY FIX DX FIX   ! a pinned support at midspan  
     CVL REF END  S 0.5 CY FIX DX FREE ! only local‐y is fixed, rotation free  
     CVL REF XI   S 0.4 CY FIX DX FREE ! using a 40% fractional location  
     CVL HDIV 4                        ! subdivide the member into 4 equal parts  
     …  
     MEMB  …  

By organizing the CVL card in this way, you can precisely locate springs or fixities anywhere along a beam, control both translational and rotational restraint, and ensure the FEM mesh conforms to your support locations.

This table defines three elemental support‐stiffness inputs (DX, CY and CZ) that apply exclusively when you follow up with a MEMB input in your model. Each entry prescribes a localized spring or torsional restraint, with a user‐specified stiffness value and a default of zero. In practice, these support parameters let you simulate elastic footing or embedment conditions on beam‐oriented elements.

1. Columns and Their Roles  
   • Item  
     – The parameter identifier that you reference in your input deck.  
     – Must be spelled exactly as shown (DX, CY, CZ).  
   • Description  
     – A concise explanation of the mechanical effect of the support.  
     – DX is torsional, CY and CZ are translational along local axes.  
   • Unit  
     – The physical unit in which the stiffness must be supplied.  
     – DX: kNm/m/rad (torsional stiffness per unit length and per radian)  
     – CY & CZ: kN/m² (translational stiffness per unit area)  
   • Default  
     – The assumed stiffness if you omit this item from your input.  
     – All three default to 0, i.e. no restraint.

2. Row‐by‐Row Explanation  
   – DX (Torsional support)  
     • Applies a spring that resists twist about the beam’s local x-axis.  
     • Useful for modelling rotational restraint from flanges, shear walls or diaphragms.  
     • Unit is kNm/m/rad: you supply the stiffness per metre of beam length, per radian of rotation.  
     • Default = 0 (free torsion).  
     • Special note: if you already have support CX or support CY creating torsional restraint, you must manually include any flange flexural stiffness in your DX value to capture the combined effect.  
   – CY (Support in local y-direction)  
     • A linear elastic spring resisting translation along the beam’s local y-axis.  
     • Use to simulate lateral soil pressure, guide bearings, or distributed shelf contact.  
     • Unit is kN/m²: stiffness per unit area.  
     • Default = 0 (no support in y).  
   – CZ (Support in local z-direction)  
     • A linear elastic spring resisting translation along the beam’s local z-axis.  
     • Suited for modelling vertical support pads, grout layers, or bearing plates.  
     • Same unit as CY (kN/m²).  
     • Default = 0 (no support in z).

3. Context of Use  
   • These parameters are inactive until you issue a MEMB record. MEMB triggers membrane‐type behavior and activates the DX/CY/CZ supports on the element.  
   • See also: MEMB and CV for related inputs controlling membrane forces and sectional stiffness.  
   • If your structural model already imposes rotational restraint through other means (e.g., CV springs in bending directions), remember to superpose flange flexural contributions into DX to avoid underestimating the total torsional stiffness.

4. Practical Tips for RAG Indexing  
   • Tag each item name (DX, CY, CZ) as a distinct retrieval key.  
   • Record units and default values as metadata fields (“unit”: “kN/m²”, “default”: “0”).  
   • Highlight the MEMB‐dependency in the description field so that vector searches about “activated only after MEMB” will surface these entries.  
   • Include the cross‐reference “See also: MEMB, CV” to facilitate semantic linking in your knowledge graph.

The table shown defines the four fields you must supply whenever you declare a numeric variable via the TVAR input record in SOFiSTiK.  It summarizes each field’s name, purpose, data‐type or unit, and the default behavior if you omit it.

Overall record purpose  
• TVAR lets you introduce a pure numeric variable within a freely selectable scope (SCOP).  
• You cannot use it to define literals, tables or functions—only numbers (or expressions that evaluate to numbers).  
• Once defined, the variable remains “in memory” for all subsequent input until you override it with another TVAR of the same NAME.

Field‐by‐field description  
1. NAME  
  – Description: The identifier of your variable.  
  – Unit/Data type: Lit16 (up to 16 characters).  
  – Default: “!” (mandatory—you must supply a name).  
  – Notes:  
    • Must conform to SOFiSTiK’s literal naming rules (letters, digits, hyphens, no spaces).  
    • Common practice: use a mnemonic that relates to Eurocode boxed values (e.g. GAM-S0, KFCT, ALFAM).  

2. VAL  
  – Description: The numeric value or an arithmetic expression to be evaluated.  
  – Unit/Data type: Lit64 (up to 64 characters, to accommodate longer expressions).  
  – Default: “!” (mandatory—you must supply something here).  
  – Notes:  
    • If you precede the entry with “=” you may input a formula (e.g. =1.2*0.85).  
    • If you supply a pure number, it is taken literally.  
    • The expression may use previously defined variables (global or in‐scope).  

3. SCOP  
  – Description: The variable’s scope—i.e. where in the input deck it remains visible.  
  – Unit/Data type: none (free text token).  
  – Default: “*” (local scope only for this record; not stored to database).  
  – Notes:  
    • If you omit SCOP or use “*”, the variable lives only in the immediate processing context.  
    • To push the variable into the database for later retrieval, supply a scope name (e.g. DESI, GEOM).  
    • In typical Eurocode design runs you might do:  
        TVAR NAME GAM-S0 VAL 1.0 SCOP DESI  
        TVAR NAME GAM-S1 VAL 1.1 SCOP DESI  

4. CMNT  
  – Description: A free‐text comment or explanation attached to your variable.  
  – Unit/Data type: Lit32 (up to 32 characters).  
  – Default: “–” (no comment).  
  – Notes:  
    • Useful for documenting why you chose a nonstandard national factor or for linking back to a clause in a National Annex.  
    • This comment will appear in the database listing and input listing.  

How it ties into the workflow  
– TVAR must appear before any input records that reference the variable (e.g. in cross‐section definitions, load definitions or design commands).  
– If you define the same NAME twice in the same scope, the later definition overrides the earlier one.  
– Variables defined with TVAR can be used inside expressions for section classification (AQB), lateral–torsional buckling parameters (β, λLT,0), safety factors (GAM-S0, GAM-S1), or any other numeric input field that accepts =expressions.  
– When you switch design codes (CTRL …), those scoped variables remain active unless you explicitly reinitialize them.  

By following this field‐by‐field specification, you ensure that your TVAR records are syntactically correct, well documented, and behave predictably in subsequent design modules.

     – Both kₙ and C₁ are then picked directly from the tabulated values.

6. Enveloping results store (load‐case storage):  
   • CTRL LCST <nr>  
   – Specifies a special load‐case number in which the maximum utilization ratios from all subsequent designs are collected.  
   – CTRL LCST 0 clears the envelope storage.  

7. Interaction with TVAR and boxed values:  
   • Although “TVAR” (scope-limited numeric variables) and boxed Eurocode values (e.g. GAM-S0, GAM-S1) can be defined globally via STO# or LET#, CTRL operates at the procedural level. It does not define new variables but reads those global or INI‐file values and adjusts the calculation flow accordingly.

8. LC (Loadcase selection) record summary:  
   • Record name: LC  
   • NO: Loadcase number to be activated for design (integer)  
   • Default: 1  
   • Unit: –  
   • Purpose: Selects which pre‐computed loadcase is to be treated by subsequent MEMB design calls.  

In practice, you would precede your MEMB definitions with one or more CTRL records to set national annex factors (via TVAR if needed), cross-section rules and buckling options. Only once the desired combination of standards (EN 1993-1-1, DIN 18800-2/OEN 4300, BS 5950-1) and numeric parameters is established do you switch to LC to pick the individual loadcases for which the steel members will be designed.

The table shown defines the CTRL parameters available when performing member design according to EN 1993-1-1 in the SOFiSTiK BDK module.  Each line of the table corresponds to a keyword (EN column) that controls a specific aspect of the lateral-torsional buckling checks, sway considerations, load-case selection or design method.  The four columns are:

  • EN: the keyword to be used in the input file (“BETA”, “LLT0”, etc.)  
  • Description: what the keyword governs, with references to clauses in EN 1993-1-1  
  • Unit: none of these parameters carry physical units (they are nondimensional settings)  
  • Default: the value assumed if the keyword is omitted

Below is a detailed breakdown of each parameter:

1. BETA  
   – Defines both cross-section classification and the β factor in the buckling resistance formula.  
   – Options “1”, “2”, “3” or “AUTO” follow clause 6.3.2.3 for rolled or equivalent welded shapes.  
   – Options “G1”, “G2”, “G3” or “AUTO:G” follow clause 6.3.2.2 (“general case”).  
   – If a numeric β is needed directly (clause 6.3.2.3), it is taken here.  
   – Default: 0.75  

2. LLT0  
   – The reference slenderness λ_LT,0 used in the lateral-torsional buckling check (clause 6.3.2.3).  
   – Default: 0.4  

3. TAB  
   – Activates use of the correction factor k_c from Table 6.6 in EN 1993-1-1 (clause 6.3.2.3).  
   – Keyword value “YES” forces k_c and C1 to come from the eight discrete cases in that table; “NO” (default) uses the continuous eigenvalue-based calculation.  
   – Default: NO  

4. LCST  
   – Specifies a load-case number in which the enveloped design results (max utilisation ratios) will be stored.  
   – If set to 0, no further design results overwrite a previously defined LCST.  
   – Default: – (none)  

5. SWY / SWZ  
   – Toggles consideration of sway in the local y or z-direction (EC 3, Method 2).  
   – Set to “YES” to include sway; “NO” omits sway effects.  
   – Both default to NO.  

6. LTB  
   – Defines whether the member is “susceptible to torsional deformations” (i.e. lateral-torsional buckling) under EC 3 Method 2.  
   – “AUTO” (default) leaves the decision to the internal classification and buckling analysis.  

7. MTHD  
   – Selects EC 3 design method: 1 or 2.  
   – Method 1 corresponds to Annex A; Method 2 to Annex B.  
   – Default: 1  

How it ties together:  
When you invoke CTRL in your BDK input, these settings remain active for all subsequent MEMB records until they are overridden by a new CTRL line.  By default, BDK will automatically classify the cross-section (via an internal AQB step), assume the default lateral-torsional parameters (β = 0.75, λ_LT,0 = 0.4) and compute k_c continuously.  Specifying TAB=YES, or choosing AUTO:G vs. AUTO, or switching to Method 2, all adjust how EN 1993-1-1’s clauses 6.3.2.2–6.3.2.3 and Tables 6.4–6.6 are applied in your design.

The table excerpt under the heading “DIN” is part of the BDK program’s CTRL‐record definitions for controlling parameters in steel‐design checks (particularly lateral–torsional buckling and general system factors) according to Eurocode EN 1993-1-1, DIN 18800-2 and BS 5950-1. It consists of four columns—parameter name (DIN), description, unit, and default value—and six rows, each defining one control variable. Below is a detailed breakdown suitable for indexing in a RAG vector store:

1. Column Structure  
   • DIN (Parameter Name)  
     – The keyword used in the CTRL input record.  
   • Description  
     – A short statement of what the parameter controls or represents, often referencing the relevant Eurocode clause or table.  
   • Unit  
     – The physical dimension (if any). A dash “–” indicates dimensionless quantities.  
   • Default  
     – The value assumed if the parameter is not explicitly set. An asterisk (*) indicates that the default is code-dependent or must be supplied elsewhere (e.g. by the INI file).

2. Parameter Entries  
   1. BMY  
      • Description: βMy moment coefficient for lateral torsional buckling under primary bending.  
      • Reference: Eurocode EN 1993-1-1 Chapter 3.5.1, Table 11.  
      • Unit: dimensionless.  
      • Default: “*” (taken from the code’s INI file or earlier CTRL definitions).  
      • Role: Influences the reduction factor for major-axis bending buckling checks.  
   2. BMZ  
      • Description: βMz coefficient for lateral torsional buckling under transverse bending in the global z-direction.  
      • Reference: analogous to BMY, EN 1993-1-1.  
      • Unit: dimensionless.  
      • Default: “*” (code-provided).  
      • Role: Similar to BMY but for the weak axis.  
   3. BMQY  
      • Description: βM,Qy moment coefficient for transverse loading in the global y-direction (Chapter 3.5.1, Table 11).  
      • Unit: dimensionless.  
      • Default: 1.35  
      • Role: Applies to combined bending checks when major bending is due to transverse loads.  
   4. BMQZ  
      • Description: βM,Qz analogous coefficient for transverse loading in the global z-direction.  
      • Unit: dimensionless.  
      • Default: 1.35  
      • Role: Used in weak-axis transverse bending buckling evaluations.  
   5. SFAC  
      • Description: System factor n, which accounts for degree of static indeterminacy (Chapter 3.3.4, Table 9).  
      • Unit: dimensionless.  
      • Default: 2.5  
      • Role: Adjusts the global safety factor depending on whether the structure is statically determinate or indeterminate.  
   6. LCST  
      • Description: Load‐case number for collecting and storing enveloped results. When present, the maximum utilization per member is saved to this load‐case identifier.  
      • Unit: dimensionless.  
      • Default: “–” (none; if omitted no new result set is created).  
      • Role: Directs the program to produce a separate load‐case envelope in WinGRAF or Result Viewer.

3. Usage Notes  
   • All of these CTRL parameters remain in effect for subsequent MEMB records until overridden by a new CTRL.  
   • BMY and BMZ default to code tables unless explicitly overridden—this allows customization for special national annexes.  
   • LCST 0 resets the result‐store feature, preventing further envelopes from being appended to the previously specified load‐case.  
   • The combination of BMY/BMZ and BMQY/BMQZ controls whether lateral torsional buckling curves, correction factors kc and C1, and section classifications (AUTO, AUTO:G, class 1–4) follow the general or default EN 1993-1-1 cases.

By capturing each parameter’s name, role, numeric default, and relevant code reference, this description supports both human understanding and machine retrieval in a RAG vector store.

The table below defines the four optional sub-parameters of the “BS” input group used by the BDK “CTRL” module to control cross-section classification and lateral-torsional buckling coefficients. All entries remain in effect for subsequent MEMB records until they are overridden.

1. Field name (column “BS”)  
   – SCL  
     • Description: Selects the cross-section class to be used for design checks under EN 1993-1-1 or BS 5950. Valid entries are:  
       – 1, 2 or 3 : fix the section class explicitly (Class 1 = plastic, Class 2 = compact, Class 3 = slender)  
       – AUTO : perform automatic classification according to AQB (if AQB is not run separately, BDK will call it internally).  
     • Unit: –  
     • Default: AUTO  
     • Notes:

       – Specifying AUTO:G forces the “general case” rules of EN 1993-1-1 § 6.3.2.2 (allowed only in conjunction with a G1-G3 manual override).  

   – BMY

     • Unit: –  
     • Default: * (take βMy from the code’s INI file for the selected design standard)  
     • Notes:  
       – If omitted, BDK uses the code‐prescribed default:  
         • For the default (6.3.2.3) case: βMy = 0.75  
         • For the general case (6.3.2.2) via G1-G3: βMy = 1.00  

   – BMZ  
     • Description: βMz, the moment‐gradient coefficient for lateral-torsional buckling about the weak axis (secondary or transverse bending).  
     • Unit: –  
     • Default: * (take βMz from the code’s INI file)

     • Description: Loadcase number under which the enveloped (maximum) member utilization from the design run will be stored. This allows you to output design results for a specific envelope loadcase in WinGRAF or the Result Viewer.  
     • Unit: –  
     • Default: – (no LCST is set by default; results aren’t assigned to a specific envelope case)  
     • Usage:  
       – Any subsequent CTRL/BDK design will record its maximum u-values to the specified LCST.  
       – To clear or stop recording, specify LCST 0.  

General behavior: once any of these BS parameters is defined under a CTRL input record, they remain active for all following MEMB definitions until they are changed by a new CTRL record.

It uses a combination of colored and shaded boxes, arrows and simple beam sketches to guide the reader through the calculation logic:

1. A pink, rounded‐corner box at the very top is labeled “START.” From its bottom edge, a single dark gray arrow leads downward to the first analysis step.

2. On the right side, aligned with that arrow, is a large white rectangular process box (black outline) containing:
   • A small beam sketch: a horizontal line supported at its left end by a pinned support icon (triangle) and on the right end by a roller icon (circle on horizontal line).  
   • A downward‐pointing blue arrow at midspan indicating an applied vertical load.  
   • A red, triangular‐filled region below the beam (“load diagram”) emphasizing a distributed or concentrated load.  
   • Above this sketch the text reads “System definition: boundary conditions and applied loads.”  
   An arrow labeled “Eigenvalue Analysis →” points leftward from this box.

3. On the left side of the chart, directly opposite that arrow, is a small gray trapezoidal box (slanted top and bottom) labelled “M_cr.” This represents the critical moment obtained from the first eigenvalue buckling analysis. A dark gray arrow continues downward from this “M_cr” block.

4. Part way down, that arrow meets a second white rectangular process box on the right. This box is similar in style to the first but its contents differ:
   • A beam sketch again supported pinned–roller.  
   • A curved blue arrow wrapped around each end of the beam signifying pure bending (i.e. a “virtual moment”).  
   • A red rectangular block under the beam representing a constant bending moment distribution.  
   • Above the sketch is the legend “Create virtual bending moment (M = constant).”  
   From the right side of this box, another arrow labelled “Eigenvalue Analysis →” points left.

5. Opposite that arrow is another gray trapezoidal box labelled “M_cr,0,” denoting the critical buckling moment from the second, pure-moment eigenvalue analysis. A second arrow from “M_cr,0” rejoins the earlier arrow coming down from the first “M_cr,” forming a single downward arrow.

6. That combined arrow enters a small gray rectangle (square‐cornered) bearing the formula  
   C₁ = M_cr / M_cr,0  

7. Beneath that box, a final arrow leads to a pink rounded‐corner box labeled “END.”

Flow and color coding:
 • Pink boxes mark the start and end of the procedure.  
 • White process boxes (with black borders) describe the actions or model setups.  
 • Gray trapezoidal boxes capture key numeric results (M_cr and M_cr,0).  
 • Arrows carry the logical progression: first eigenvalue → M_cr, second eigenvalue → M_cr,0 → compute C₁.

This diagram succinctly shows how BDK (SOFiSTiK’s buckling design kernel) determines the C₁ factor by comparing the system’s true critical buckling moment to that of an idealized constant-moment (pure bending) case.

Below is a comprehensive, field‐by‐field breakdown of the MEMB input table as used in BDK for beam or truss analyses. This description will help you index and retrieve the right parameter definitions in a RAG‐style vector store.

1. General Context  
   • The MEMB record is the final input block that triggers a continuous deflection‐curve analysis on a series of structural lines or beams.  
   • If you need to chain multiple structural lines into one “member,” you can use the CONT keyword.  
   • As of version 2020, you can also reference pre‐defined design elements (from DECREATOR) by their ID in the MEMB record.

2. Table Columns  
   • Item: The keyword you use in the MEMB input.  
   • Description: What that keyword means and how it affects the analysis.  
   • Unit: The expected data type or unit (often literal, LIT, or dimensionless).  
   • Default: The value assumed if you omit this keyword.

3. Field Descriptions

• REF (Reference type)  
  – Description: Specifies how the member is defined. Options are:  
     • BEAM – use individual beam numbers  
     • SLN  – structural line numbers  
     • TRUS – truss numbers  
     • CONT – continuation record (to append additional segments)  
  – Unit: Literal (LIT)  
  – Default: CONT  

• FROM (Start index)  
  – Description: Indicates the first element number or structural line in the member sequence. If you are using a range, this is the lower bound.  
  – Unit: none  
  – Default: 1  

• TO (End index)  
  – Description: Marks the last element number in the continuous sequence. Ignored if you use explicit CONT entries.  
  – Unit: none  
  – Default: same as FROM (i.e. single‐element member)  

• INC (Increment)  
  – Description: Step size between element numbers when generating a range (FROM to TO).  
  – Unit: none  
  – Default: 1  

• SKY (Buckling length factor, major axis)  
  – Description: User‐supplied effective length factor for flexural buckling about the major axis. Overrides code defaults if provided.  
  – Unit: none  
  – Default: “–” (i.e. let the code compute it)  

• SKZ (Buckling length factor, minor axis)  
  – Description: Same as SKY but for the minor (transverse) axis.  
  – Unit: none  
  – Default: “–”  

• TYPE (Analysis type)  
  – Description: Selects which internal check to perform. Options are:  
     • FLEX – centric compression only  
     • LAT  – major‐axis bending (lateral‐torsional buckling check)  
     • LTB  – combined bending & axial compression  
     • EIGE – eigenvalue extraction (buckling loads)  
  – Unit: Literal (LIT)  
  – Default: LAT  

• ID (Design‐Element ID)  
  – Description: A numerical identifier for a pre‐defined design element (created via DECREATOR) or, if omitted, BDK uses the SLN number. If multiple design elements exist, enter the exact ID here.  
  – Unit: none  
  – Default: SLN number  

4. Usage Notes  
   – Always place MEMB records last. Any CONT lines immediately following the MEMB line are treated as part of the same member.  
   – Avoid inserting supports or point loads between concatenated structural lines, or the deflection curve will not be continuous.  
   – When invoking a design element by ID (with TYPE=EIGE, for example), be sure you have run DECREATOR first to define that element.

The table excerpt defines two related ECHO-command parameters used by the BDK (Buckling Design Kit) for controlling which types of results are returned and how much detail is included. Both parameters are literal fields (Unit = LIT), and neither has an implicit default value in the table itself (Default = “–”), but broader default behaviors are described in the surrounding documentation.

1. OPT (Option Selector)  
   • Purpose: Specifies which categories of analysis results should be output.  
   • Unit: LIT (a literal keyword)  
   • Default: none listed here; actual defaults are governed by the general ECHO defaults (see below).  
   • Allowed literals and their meanings:  
     ‑ FORC: design forces and bending moments  
     ‑ SECT: sectional (geometric) values of members  
     ‑ MAT: material properties  
     ‑ BOUN: support or boundary‐condition definitions  
     ‑ EIGE: buckling eigenvalues  
     ‑ MEMB: buckling resistance checks for steel members  
     ‑ SUM: summary of all results  
     ‑ FULL: shorthand for selecting every available option  
     ‑ DESE: design elements listing  
     ‑ CLAS: cross-section classification data  
     ‑ PLOT: graphical (member) representation output  

2. VAL (Output Extent)  
   • Purpose: Determines the verbosity or extent of the selected output categories.  
   • Unit: LIT (a literal keyword)  
   • Default: none listed here; default verbosity is “YES” (normal output) for most options, with exceptions noted below.  
   • Allowed literals and their meanings:  
     ‑ NO: suppress all output for the categories specified by OPT  
     ‑ YES: produce normal (default) output  
     ‑ FULL: produce extended output with additional intermediate details  
     ‑ EXTR: produce extreme, highly detailed output  

Additional Context and Default Behavior  
• Unless overridden by VAL, every OPT choice will yield normal output (YES) by default. Two notable exceptions:  
  – EIGE (buckling eigenvalues) defaults to NO output (i.e., eigenvalues are not printed unless VAL is set to YES or higher).  
  – SUM (summary) defaults to EXTR (extreme output), ensuring the summary is as detailed as possible unless altered.  
• From BDK version 2020 onward, the MEMB and/or PLOT options automatically include member-plot generation. Plotting can be turned off explicitly by issuing “ECHO PLOT NO.”  
• The “Chapter 4: Output Description” section of the BDK manual provides deeper insight into what each level of VAL (YES/FULL/EXTR) adds in terms of tables, intermediate calculation steps, and plotting details.

How This Table Fits into a RAG-Friendly Vector Store  
• Fields (columns) become named metadata axes: “Item,” “Description,” “Unit,” “Default.”  
• Each OPT literal and VAL literal can be stored as distinct concept tokens with attached descriptive text.  
• The additional context—default behaviors, version-specific changes, pointer to Chapter 4—can be incorporated as supplementary context documents to support retrieval‐augmented generation and precise answer grounding.

ECHO
 All options have a normal extent of output as default, except of EIGE with a default of no output and SUM with an extreme output as default. The effect of the individual options can be seen in Chapter 4: Output Description.
 From version 2020 per default, BDK will activate the member plots. This may be deactivated by using ECHO PLOT NO.

The input table is a comprehensive summary of all design forces, moments, section properties and resistance values for each beam element in a structural model. It is organized section-by-section along each beam’s longitudinal axis (x), and contains the following groups of information:

1. Identification & Position  
 • Beam number: unique identifier for each beam element  
 • Section coordinate x [m]: distance along the beam where the section data is reported  
 • Cross-section number: links to the cross-section database  
 • Material number: links to the material database (e.g. for Young’s modulus, yield strength)

2. Section Geometric Properties  
 • Cross-sectional area A [m²]  
 • Torsional constant J [m⁴] (torsional moment of inertia)  
 • Warping constant Cw [m⁶] (resistance to section warping under torsion)  
 • Second moments of area Iy, Iz [m⁴] about the local y- and z-axes

3. Design Internal Forces & Moments (all in kN or kNm)  
 • N: axial (normal) force  
 • Vy, Vz: shear forces in local y- and z-directions  
 • Mt (Mx): torsional moment about the longitudinal axis  
 • My, Mz: bending moments about the local y- and z-axes  
 • Mt2: secondary torsional moment (warping‐related torsion)

4. Resistance & Capacity Values  
 • N_Rd: design plastic resistance to axial compression (kN)  
 • M_pl,y,Rk; M_pl,z,Rk: characteristic plastic bending resistances about y and z (kNm)

The input “Buckling Eigenvalues” table is organized into a series of thematic blocks, each capturing a different aspect of the member’s buckling behavior, design checks and auxiliary terms. Its overall purpose is to record, compute and report the key parameters that govern flexural, lateral, torsional and interaction buckling for compression members in steel structures. Below is a detailed breakdown of its structure:

1. Table Header  
  • Title: “BUCKLING EIGENVALUES”  
  • Subtitle: “TYPE” and “Type of eigenvalue analysis” indicate whether the row refers to flexural buckling, lateral buckling, lateral–torsional buckling or a mixed‐mode analysis (denoted by codes such as FLEX, LAT, LTB).  
  • “No.” / “Eigenvalue number” gives the sequence index for multiple buckling modes per loadcase.

2. Loadcase Information  
  • Loadcase number (Loadcase) links the buckling output to a specific combination of applied forces and moments.  
  • N-Ed [kN]: design axial force (negative values indicate compression).  
  • M-y,Ed [kNm], M-z,Ed [kNm]: absolute maximum bending moments about the y–y and z–z principal axes respectively.

3. Flexural Buckling (Elastic Critical Forces and Lengths)  
  • N-cr [kN]: elastic critical flexural buckling force.  
  • L-cr [m]: calculated comparative buckling length (effective length) in the relevant axis.  
  • Buckling curve for cross-section (y–y or z–z) with associated α (imperfection factor), λ (non-dimensional slenderness) and χ (reduction factor).  
  • N-b,Rd [kN]: design buckling resistance under axial load (reduced by χ).

4. Lateral–Torsional Buckling  
  • M-cr [kNm]: elastic critical moment for lateral–torsional buckling.  
  • C-1: moment gradient factor (based on bending diagram and end restraint).  
  • LTB recommended curve (α-LT imperfection factor, λ-LT slenderness, λ-LT0 plateau length).  
  • β: correction factor for the lateral–torsional buckling curve.  
  • χ-LT: reduction factor (with optional k-c moment distribution factor and f modification factor yielding χ-LT,mod).  
  • M-b,Rd [kNm]: design buckling resistance moment.

5. Interaction Factors  
  • k-yy, k-yz, k-zy, k-zz: factors that account for cross‐interaction between bending axes and axial load when combining utilization ratios.

6. Auxiliary Terms for Torsional and Combined Modes  
  • λ-0: slenderness parameter for buckling due to uniform bending.  
  • N-cr,T [kN]: elastic critical torsional buckling force.  
  • C-my,0, C-mz,0: equivalent uniform moment factors used in non-uniform bending checks.  
  • Non-dimensional slenderness for lateral–torsional buckling repeated for context in combined checks.

7. Utilisation Checks  
  • CHECK OF FLEXURAL BUCKLING/TORSIONAL BUCKLING:  
     – n-y = N-Ed / N-b,y,Rd, n-z = N-Ed / N-b,z,Rd  
  • CHECK OF LATERAL BUCKLING:  
     – m-y = M-y,Ed / M-b,Rd  
  • CHECK OF LATERAL–TORSIONAL BUCKLING:  
     – m-y, m-z, n-y, n-z ratios as above, plus combined utilization indices nm-y and nm-z per EN 1993-1-1 Eqs. 6.61 and 6.62.

8. Printing Control Flags  
  • NO / YES / FULL: specify whether this table is omitted, printed partially (only design values) or printed in full detail depending on the selected output mode (FLEX, LAT, LTB).

9. Steel Members Metadata (beginning of next section)  
  Although truncated in the input snapshot, this section lists global properties such as:  
  • Selection type and sign convention  
  • Total length of the member  
  • Cross-section number and class  
  • Partial safety factors, etc.
